A daily report of the names that are starting to surge in AI: new models, products, tools and repos, caught where they are said first, before they show up in keyword tools. Built for people who make pages, posts or products around new terms: SEO for AI tool sites, newsletters, directories, anyone who wants to know about "Strata" or "Seedance" the day it appears and not two weeks later. ## Why A new name leaves a trail, in this order: 1. A lab or a well-followed account says it on X; a model enters Hugging Face's trending list. 2. One GitHub repo takes off on its own. 3. Directories and competitors add pages for it; someone registers a domain for it and the site starts to rank. 4. Your own site gets its first search impressions for it. 5. Google Trends shows the curve, days or weeks later. Keyword tools read step 5. This radar reads steps 1 to 4 every day and uses step 5 only to check itself. One example it was built around: [Niko1221/Strata](https://github.com/Niko1221/Strata) was created on 2026-09-24 and had 7,700 stars nine days later. People were searching "niko strata" from 9/26, while no second repo carried the name and no keyword tool listed it. A single repo gaining 800 stars a day is the whole signal, and it is public. ## What it reads ![How the radar works: six signals, a name judge, the keyword table with its page-one check, a daily report and a 14-day check; used from the command line, three Agent Skills, an MCP server or the pains command. What 0.6.0 added is purple and tagged NEW](docs/radar.en.gif) Purple, tagged NEW: what 0.6.0 added. On the keyword table: word age, markets, page-one shape, the twelve months, your own rank, what else holds page one (threads, an AI overview) and the exact-match .com. The first words ③'s new sites rank for, what ChatGPT recommends for ⑦'s asks, three more payment platforms and the builders on ⑧, ⑨ just listed, ⑩ money and the evidence beside the names. With the example config (35 X accounts read three times a day, the keyword table for 5 names a day) a month costs about $15: $10 for the X reads, $5 for the keyword table. Read fewer accounts, or read them once a day, and it drops in proportion. ## The keyword table A name is half of what you need. "SynthID Detector" has a short life as a keyword and belongs to Google; the job it does, "ai image detector", is what people keep searching, and nobody owns it. Each day the radar reads the new names once more and writes one table with both: ``` | Keyword | Type | Behind | New? | Est. searches/day | Started rising | Peak vs gpts | Peak day | Last 7 days vs the 7 before | Now | First searched | Markets (searches/KD) | Page one | Page-one shape | Decision | | **photocraft** 🖼 | name | — | yes | 12747 | 2026-10-05 | 97 vs 3.1 | 2026-10-09 | — | still rising | 2026-10-04 🆕 | **best US** · US 110/0 · DE 20/0 · FR 20/0 · JP 10/31 | — | beatable · 1 home / 6 inner · 2 platform · exact title ×6 | **prioritize** | | **ai image detector** 🖼 | generic | synthid detector | no | 2537 | — | 87 vs 31.6 | 2026-10-04 | ×1.2 | flat | 2023-02-19 | **best US** · US 74k/37 · DE 3.6k/48 · FR 2.9k/47 · JP 720/31 | — | — | watch | | **photoshop alternative** ⚠ | generic | photocraft | no | 244 | — | 61 vs 61.7 | 2026-10-08 | ×1.8 | flat | — | — | — | — | skip | ``` (a real run, 2026-10-12, shortened; the Page one column came later, and First searched, Markets and Page-one shape in 0.6.0, from a run of 2026-10-18, see below. 0.6.0 also adds a `12 months` column after `Now` and an action after the decision, `→ update yours`, `→ improve yours` or `→ new page`: 10 to 13 below.) How it is made (`radar/usecases.py`): 1. **Evidence**: the most-liked posts that mention the name (X advanced search) and, for a repository, its README. 2. **Phrases**: a model reads the evidence and writes the keyword an ordinary person would type for each job it sees people doing, with a quote that backs it. A phrase built on another product's name ("photoshop alternative") is kept and marked ⚠: demand often hangs on the incumbent, and whether to use someone's brand is your call. With a GoAnyAPI key (optional, below) the radar also takes **Google Trends' related queries** for the name: what people really searched together with it. For SynthID Detector that gave "ai photo detector", "google ai detector" and "ai detector"; these rows carry 🔎. Queries that hold the name are listed as its long-tails ("photocraft download", "nano banana 2.1 vs pro"). Queries that are themselves the names of other rising things ("gpt image 2.5" beside "nano banana 2.1") are kept as leads of their own. 3. **Screen**: a second call scores how well the name answers each phrase, marks brands, and spots the names of other things; the loosely related ones are dropped. For Claude Haiku 5.5 it dropped all six proposed ("ai coding assistant", "github copilot alternative"); for SynthID Detector it kept all five. 4. **Volume**: Google Ads monthly searches for the rest, one batch call. Phrases under `min_volume` are dropped; most are. 5. **Trends**, twice per row: the term alone gives the shape (new or not, the day it started rising, the peak, the last week against the week before, what it is doing now); the term beside a benchmark keyword (`gpts` by default) gives the size. 6. **Page one**, for the rows that would be acted on (eight at most): Google's first page (about $0.002 a keyword), the rating of each site on it (GoAnyAPI, $0.002 a site, kept 30 days) and the keyword difficulty ($0.012 a call). With a GoAnyAPI key also who already builds for the term and who pays for it: the pages Google holds with it in the title from the last month (`pages built`) and the domains running Google ads on it (`advertisers`, from Ads transparency), $0.008 a row. `open` = three or more of the ten results sit on sites rated under 30, or difficulty under 20; `crowded` = none does and difficulty is 40 or more; `mixed` in between. Under the table it names the weakest site on page one, where a new page can get in, and what kinds of pages hold it (tools, lists, articles, videos, forums). Ads on the page mean someone pays for that click. Recorded only, in report.json as `page_age` and not used in any decision yet: how old the sites on page one are (each domain's registration, from RDAP, free) and which results entered the top 10 since the reading before, to check later whether a page one with young sites on it is one a new site gets onto. 7. **Word age**, for the prioritize and watch rows: the term's Trends interest over five years (one point a week); the first week with any interest is `First searched`, and 🆕 marks a term first searched in the last 180 days. A new term's page one is read one step easier (crowded → mixed, mixed → open): difficulty scores and site ratings are made from pages written for something else and lag a word nobody searched half a year ago. The week still running and Trends' unsettled last two days are left out, so a "0, 100" tail cannot make an old word look new. One Trends task a row, $0.0012. A term made of words people searched before ("nano banana" reads a little interest in 2021) is dated by those older searches. 8. **Markets**, for the same rows: Google Ads monthly searches in each market of `markets.codes` (US, DE, FR, JP by default; all languages) and, with `difficulty` on, the keyword difficulty there, in one compact cell: `best DE · US 5k/50 · DE 900/5 · FR 300 · JP 0 · top Germany`. `best` = the most searches per point of difficulty when every market with searches has a difficulty, else the most searches. `top` = the country where Trends interest is highest, among the major markets (Trends measures a share of local searches, and on its own puts Sint Maarten first). About $0.41 a run with the defaults (a $0.09 volume call per market, about $0.012 a difficulty call), plus $0.0024 a row for the top region. 9. **Page-one shape**, for the prioritized rows: the live top ten (US / en / desktop by default; the page-one check's own results are reused, so it usually costs nothing extra, otherwise about $0.002 a term) read as homepages against inner pages, results on high-authority platforms (`serp_shape.platforms`: github.com, medium.com, sites.google.com, `*.github.io`, reddit.com, youtube.com, wikipedia.org) and titles that hold the keyword. `platform-held` = half or more on platforms; `beatable` = mostly inner pages and no exact-match homepage (a homepage titled with the term, or whose domain spells it); `contested` otherwise. Under the table it lists the URL and title of #1 and #2. Each of the three has `"enabled": false` in its config block to turn it off. On 2026-10-18, for "photocraft" (prioritize) and "ai image detector" (watch), they read: first searched 2026-10-04 🆕 and 2023-02-19; best market US for both (74k searches and KD 37 for "ai image detector"); page one of "photocraft" `beatable · 1 home / 6 inner · 2 platform · exact title ×6`, held at #1 by the GitHub repository. The run cost $0.42. Four more readings came in 0.6.0 too. None of them buys anything: they read what the volume call and the page-one check already brought back, your own Search Console, and the .com registry. 10. **12 months** (`year_curve`), every row with Google Ads data: the volume call already carries each phrase's last twelve months. The column draws them as bars on the term's own scale from zero and adds a word: `new since` (barely searched a year ago), `peaked` (a burst past its top: twice its median month or more, at half of it or less now), `falling`, `rising` (the last three months against the three before, ±30%) or `steady`; under 50 searches in its best month it says `few searches`, since Google Ads rounds small volumes. The newest month is one to two months behind. On 2026-10-20 "claude skills" read `peaked 2026-03, now -80%` (90,500 a month at the top, 18,100 in 2026-09), "best claude skills" `new since 2026-01 · falling, -47% in 6 mo`, and "skill md" `steady`. 11. **Your rank** (`yours`), for the prioritize and watch rows: your sites (`yours.domains`, else the domain of the Search Console property in `gsc.site`) looked for in the page-one check's ten results and, with `gsc` set, in Search Console (average position, impressions and clicks for the exact query over 28 days, one call for all rows). The decision cell then says what to do: `→ update yours` (on page one by either), `→ improve yours` (a Search Console average of 11 to 30), `→ new page` (not found, or further down), and your pages are listed under the table. A rising term you already rank for is an update, not a new page. On 2026-10-20 one of our sites showed for one term at an average of 23.5 (improve that page) and for another at 89 with one impression, on its homepage (a new page). 12. **What else holds page one**, from the page-one check: its cell now names an AI overview, an answer box, a forums block, videos or news, and under the table come the forum threads on page one, best-of searches first: an answer there reaches the people searching. When Google shows an AI summary, people click a result about half as often (Pew Research Center, 2025: on 8% of visits against 15%). All five "claude skills" terms read on 2026-10-20 had an AI overview. 13. **Exact-match .com** (`dot_com`), for the prioritized rows, names first: the joined and hyphenated forms asked of the registry's RDAP (Verisign), free. Not registered is not always the usual price: registrars hold some names back or sell them as premium. Of the ten forms of five "claude skills" terms, one was free on 2026-10-20. Each has `"enabled"` in its own config block; the page-one marks come with the page-one check. On 2026-10-20 five terms cost $0.11 in all, which was the volume call and the page-one check. Searches a day are estimates. A generic term's come from its own Google Ads volume, moved to today along its own Trends curve. The benchmark is then sized from those terms, and a name, which has no volume data yet, is sized against the benchmark. Decision: **prioritize** = rose in the last 30 days, still up, at least `min_daily` searches a day. **watch** = rose but smaller, too early to read, or flat with steady demand of that size. **skip** = fading, or flat and small. A `prioritize` whose page one is `crowded` becomes `watch ↓`: still rising, but page one belongs to strong sites. In a name's first week page one is still forming (news, the maker's own pages); the second reading three days later is the one to trust. Marks: 🎬 video, 🎙 voice, 🖼 image says what the thing makes, the usual order of what visitors pay for (video > voice > image > text); leads of equal standing are sorted by it. ⚡ = a post with 1,000 or more likes walks through a manual workflow or rides a trend: a one-click tool nobody has built yet. Both come from keyword rules over the lead's own words and posts; on six known names (Nano Banana, Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.5, Claude Opus 5.5, ElevenLabs v4, Qwen Image 2.1) the format came out right for all six and ⚡ fired once, on a widely shared Opus 5.5 + Blender + Unreal walkthrough. Read the posts before acting on a mark. Each name is read twice, the day it appears and three days later, because on announcement day the posts are announcements and no use shows yet. The generic terms are kept as leads and reviewed after 14 days like the names. What to expect from it, from the first eight names we ran it on: - **The names rose; most generic terms did not, within five days.** PhotoCraft, Claude Haiku 5.5 and SynthID Detector all climbed clearly. Of the generic terms behind them, one moved: "photoshop alternative" ran about 80% above its level in the US for five days after PhotoCraft appeared. The worldwide daily series the table reads showed almost nothing of it (2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 2); a US daily series from another source showed it plainly. So a flat reading from the worldwide series does not prove a term did not move. With a GoAnyAPI key the bigger rows are read from the one-country series instead, where a rise is 1.5 times the earlier level held for three days; the same run then shows "photoshop alternative" as `still rising (US)`. - The table's dependable use today is to tell you **which existing demand a new thing serves and how big it is** ("ai image detector", about 2,500 searches a day). Whether generic terms follow the names is what the 14-day review will show, and we have no result yet. - For pure model releases (Claude Haiku 5.5, Nano Banana 2.1) the evidence was announcements and benchmarks, and the phrases proposed were weak ("ai coding assistant"). It works better for products and repositories that do one job. - **The worldwide Trends series' last two days are not settled.** For unrelated terms they came back as 0 and then 100, which reads as a spike. Our first pass was fooled by exactly this; every reader in the code now drops those two days, and a rise must last two days to count. - Google Ads volumes run about two months behind. Trends reads nothing reliable for terms under a few hundred searches a month. ### When a source is missing or down The table is still written, but it gets thinner, and it says which part is missing: | What happens | What the table loses | The line it prints | |---|---|---| | No `GOANYAPI_API_KEY` (the default) | The 🔎 rows, each name's long-tails, the other names searched alongside, and the `(US)` readings. Phrases come from the model alone and every curve from the worldwide series, where a real move can read flat | "Related queries are off: set GOANYAPI_API_KEY…" | | GoAnyAPI's Trends is down (seen on its first day in use, 2026-10-12) | The same as having no key, for that run | "Related queries failed for: …" and "Country series failed, worldwide data used instead: …" | | AIsa's post search fails for a name (timeouts seen twice on 2026-10-13) | That name's posts. A repository still has its README; a model or product without one is left with the related queries only, and with no GoAnyAPI key it gets no generic terms that day | "The post search failed; this run used READMEs and related queries only: …" | | Neither posts nor a README for a name | Its generic terms; the name's own row stays | "No posts or README found for: …" | | No lead that day is a thing with a name score of 0.8 or more | The whole table | "Nothing to read today…" | | AIsa's search-volume or Trends lookup fails | The whole table: these two are not replaceable | the error, in place of the table | A thin table is not a quiet day. Read the lines under it before you conclude that nothing moved. Set `"usecases": {"per_day": 0}` or pass `--skip usecases` to turn it off. ### ⑥ Revenue: what people already pay for A product that makes money proves the demand behind it. With `TRUSTMRR_API_KEY` set (from TrustMRR's developer dashboard), the radar reads once a week (`revenue.weekday`, Monday by default) the 30 fastest-growing products with at least `min_revenue_usd` ($500) in the last 30 days and the 30 newest listings, and keeps what it saw. The newest listings mostly earn next to nothing yet; they are read to record where they start, so a product at $0 last time that earns past the floor now is called out first. Hidden listings ("Anonymous startup") are left out, and a company's legal name gives way to its site's name ("Talent Tech Global Limited" is read as gptproto). Each product's own description goes to the keyword table as evidence, so the table reads the job people pay for, not only the brand. Growth above 1,000% reads "up from near $0": on the first run most of the fastest growers had started from almost nothing. TrustMRR's API terms forbid republishing its data and building public SEO pages from it. Use the leads for your own research; do not publish the list. ### ⑦ Asks: demand said out loud Once a week the radar searches Reddit for a dozen ways people ask for a tool ("is there an AI tool", "I wish there was a tool", "how do I automate", in `asks.patterns`), keeps the posts of the last week with a score of 2 or more, and has a small model sort them: a request, a complaint, a shared solution, or other. For requests and complaints an AI tool could answer, it writes the job the way a person would search it ("add b roll automatically", "convert slides to notes"). Jobs with at least 50 searches a month are listed with their posts and get the page-one check; each becomes a lead. Most asks are too specific to have searches yet: the first real week, 84 posts held 43 asks and only two had 50 searches a month ("best ai tool for research", from a 1,034-point r/PhD thread, and "best ai tool for coding"). So the best-scored of the others are listed too, as ideas rather than keywords. A month of posts read in a trial held a request for "an AI tool to convert PowerPoint lecture slides into notes", the same job a tool-site course uses as its worked example. With `ai_answers` on (off by default; about $0.004 an answer), the jobs with searches are also put to ChatGPT, as the answer its own interface gives with search (DataForSEO's LLM scraper), and with `"engines": ["chatgpt", "google"]` to Google's AI Mode, as "What is the best tool to {job}?". A column says which tools the answers name; under the table come the sites they cite, and ✅ when one is yours. An answer that names no tool is a gap a new tool can fill in AI search; the cited sites are the pages AI search reads for the job: get listed there, or write the comparison against them. On 2026-10-20, for "convert powerpoint slides to notes", ChatGPT named Google NotebookLM, ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, and AI Mode listed Knowt, NoteGPT and Microsoft Copilot among others. Posts are for your own research: quote them, do not republish them. ### ⑧ Sellers: who just started taking money A product's first payment link says more than its launch post: someone built a thing and asked for money for it. whoismaking.money used to rank sites by the traffic they sent to Stripe's checkout (clickstream data; its last real page in the Internet Archive is from September 2025, and by March 2026 the domain served a parked page with a hidden redirect). The same kind of data is on sale through AIsa's Similarweb at about $6 for 20 rows: too dear to cover the long tail. Payment links are a cheap stand-in. They are ordinary links on the seller's own page, so the public link graph shows them with the day each first appeared. Stripe has 143,000 linking sites and Polar 1,900 (every link a payment link); for Lemon Squeezy, Gumroad and Creem only store checkouts, `/l/` products and `/payment/` pages count, since their other links point at their own marketing sites and, for Gumroad, at profile pages spam networks use. Once a week the radar reads, for each platform, the newest 100 payment links and the newest 100 sites to link to it for the first time (about $0.06 a platform), keeps the links of those new sites, and lists the sellers with their visits (GoAnyAPI) and their own home-page title and description, which also go to the keyword table as evidence. The first real run put janitorai.com, framer.com, pub.dev, Flathub and an n8n forum thread on top: user pages on big platforms that link to someone's payment link. So the linking page must be the site's own home, pricing or product page, not a post, thread or listing; the site must rank 350 or lower on DataForSEO's 0 to 1,000 scale; and above 300,000 visits a month it counts as a platform. A small model then sorts the new sellers by kind from their own words (keyword rules when it cannot), and AI and software come first, then templates, courses and the rest; within a kind the busiest first. On the first sorted run all twelve listed were software (a live-captions app for the Mac, a chat-with-PDF tool, an AI writing app for macOS, an MCP catalog, a Japanese audit SaaS among them), where traffic alone had put a Blender add-on site, a recipe blog and a design gallery first. A payment link means the site sells, not that it sells well, and checkouts made by code at payment time are not seen. A new link is not a new seller. A first version took the newest links for new sellers; on 2026-10-14 we checked them against the day each site first linked to the platform. A site that has sold for years puts the same link on every new page it makes (one carries its Stripe link on each of its well-permit pages), and two thirds of the 2,000 newest Stripe links came from such sites: of the 60 Stripe sellers that day's list showed, 17 had just started. So a seller is new by the day its site first linked to the platform (DataForSEO's referring domains), and the report says how many links came from sites that sold already. ### History: every seller back to 2019 ```bash python -m radar history pull # every site linking to the five platforms today: about $18 python -m radar history read # their home-page titles and descriptions, free python -m radar history sort # their kind, by a small model: about $0.005 for 60 sites (--rules: keywords alone, free) python -m radar history update # weekly: the sellers that appeared since the newest day, about $0.5 python -m radar history --out sellers.csv ``` `history pull` reads every site that links to each platform today, one row per site with the day it first linked: DataForSEO's one-per-domain backlinks, oldest first, 1,000 a call ($0.06). On 2026-10-14 that day matched the referring-domain first-link day for all 1,704 Polar sites both lists name alike. It stops at `--max-usd` (default 20) and resumes where it stopped. `history` alone counts sellers per month, platform and kind; `--out` writes them all to a CSV. The rows are DataForSEO's: for research, not to republish. How far back it goes, from the link graph's monthly count of sites linking for the first time (2026-10-14; one call per platform, $0.03): | Platform | Counted from | Sites since 2019 | New sites a month, May to September 2026 | Linking today | |---|---|---|---|---| | Stripe | June 2021 (a few dozen a month before) | 306,000 | 6,500 to 8,200 (14,200 in June) | 143,000 | | Gumroad | 2019 | 530,000 | 4,200 to 5,700, while 6,400 to 9,400 drop their links | 140,000 | | Lemon Squeezy | 2023 | 34,000 | 600 to 1,100 | 18,000 | | Polar | 2024 | 2,285 | 109 to 268 | 1,943 | | Creem | 2025 | 1,708 | 74 to 268 | 1,449 | Two cautions. In October 2023 Stripe's count jumped from 3,216 to 16,206, and new links from 1.2 million to 20 million the month after: the crawler grew, not the sellers. And a pull holds only sites that still link, so the older the month, the more of its sellers are missing. For Gumroad, Lemon Squeezy and Creem the monthly counts also include links to their own sites and to profiles; the pull keeps those apart (only payment links count as sellers). ### ⑧b, ⑨, ⑩ and the evidence beside the names - **⑧b Builders** (weekly, with ⑧): the badge an AI app builder puts on what it made ("Edit with Lovable", "Built with v0") and the "Powered by beehiiv" link of a new newsletter, read from the same link graph. Most of what people build with an app builder is a business's website (a pizzeria, a lawn service); only the software among them becomes a lead, the rest says what the builder is used for. - **⑨ Just listed** (daily; the paid lists weekly): each list's new entries since the radar last read it (a first run only takes the snapshot, and lists what the source itself dates as recent). The sites behind Figma, There's An AI For That and the Chrome Web Store are not read: Google's index of their new pages is. - **⑩ Money** (weekly, GoAnyAPI): a site that earns from ads names its AdSense ID in its ads.txt, and the same ID on other domains is its owner's other sites, each a niche someone already makes money in. The sites asked about are the tool sites on page one for the day's terms and the paying products of ⑥ and ⑧. An advertiser new on one of your `ad_terms` has just decided the term is worth money. - **Beside the names**: people register sites on a name before search engines list them, so the newest domains carrying a name (whois for the first two names, HTTPS certificates for the rest), its Wikipedia views against the week before, Google's own type for it ("AI agent" means Google knows the thing; a name Google knows only as something else is taken) and Discord servers about it. For a paying product, the searches for its alternatives, comparisons and price are a market someone already proved. ### ⚡ What tutorial viewers ask for For up to three leads a day marked ⚡ (a widely shared walkthrough of a manual workflow), the radar finds the top tutorial videos for the lead (GoAnyAPI), reads their comments (AIsa, $0.001 a page) and has the model pull out what viewers ask for: the steps they find too hard, the "can this be done in one click". That list is the one-click tool. It needs a GoAnyAPI key to find the videos. ## Pain points: `python -m radar pains "ai headshot"` What people complain about for a kind of tool, grouped into the gaps a new tool can fill: - low-star Chrome Web Store reviews (1 to 3 stars) of the extensions Google shows for the keyword, or of the ones you name with `--extension ID` (GoAnyAPI: 2 credits to find them, 3 a page of reviews); - Reddit posts that complain about the job or its tools ("{keyword} alternative", "{keyword} frustrating", ...; AIsa); - comments under the top tutorial videos for the keyword (AIsa). A model groups them into gaps (missing, too hard, quality, price, wants a tool), each with a count, an example and the phrase someone with that problem would search. About $0.05 a keyword. Counts are of what was read, not of the market. What it cannot read: App Store, Google Play and Trustpilot reviews (DataForSEO serves them as tasks to post and fetch later, and AIsa runs synchronous calls only); There's An AI For That's request board (a Cloudflare challenge in front of every page; getting past it would be getting past their bot protection, so the radar does not); Facebook groups (Meta closed the Groups API in April 2024, and its research library is open to approved academic and nonprofit researchers only). ## One key, and an optional second Everything the radar needs goes through [AIsa](https://go.aisa.one/yansen-zhu): X posts, DataForSEO Trends (DataForSEO's estimate of Google search interest, not Google Trends itself) and domain data, and the models that judge names and propose phrases. One key, pay per call, no subscriptions to X's API or DataForSEO. > That link is a referral link: signing up through it supports this project. The radar works the same with a key from anywhere on aisa.one. **Optional: `GOANYAPI_API_KEY`** ([goanyapi.com](https://goanyapi.com/r/ga-95708898fb)) improves the keyword table in two ways, for about $0.07 a day: it adds Google Trends' related queries for each name, and it reads the curve of the names and the bigger generic terms (1,000 searches a month or more, eight rows at most) from 30 days of daily data for one country, settled to yesterday. Those rows show the country after "Now", as in `still rising (US)`. Without the key the table is built from the model's phrases and the worldwide series alone. The service is young (first released in August 2026); in our tests calls took 20 to 55 seconds and about one in ten failed, so the radar tries twice, reports a failure in the table and carries on. That link is a referral link too. Without an AIsa key the free signals still run (Hugging Face, GitHub, sitemaps, Search Console); the report then lists every term unsorted, because nothing judges which are names. ## Quick start [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)'s `uvx` runs the radar straight from PyPI, with nothing to clone or install: ```bash export AISA_API_KEY=... # from https://go.aisa.one/yansen-zhu; or `aisa login` with the AIsa CLI uvx new-term-radar daily --out report.md # today's new names and the keyword table behind them uvx new-term-radar keywords "photocraft" # the keyword table for names you already have ``` With no `config.json` in the folder, `daily` watches the example X accounts and sitemaps that ship with the radar and keeps its snapshots in `./state`; copy [config.example.json](config.example.json) to `config.json` there and edit it to watch your own. `uvx new-term-radar@latest …` picks up a new release; `pip install new-term-radar` (or `uv tool install new-term-radar`) keeps a `new-term-radar` command installed. Python 3.10 or newer; the radar uses only the standard library. From a clone it is the same program, with the same key: ```bash git clone https://github.com/zhuyansen/new-term-radar cd new-term-radar cp config.example.json config.json # then edit: your X accounts, sitemaps, topics python -m radar daily --out report.md ``` The first run builds its snapshots: yesterday's X vocabulary, star counts and sitemap URLs do not exist yet, so only GitHub breakouts (which need no yesterday) are reported. From the second run on, every signal reports what changed. Two commands (without a clone, `uvx new-term-radar` in place of `python -m radar`): ```bash python -m radar sources --out sources.md # ① only: X and Hugging Face. Run every few hours. python -m radar daily --skip x,hf --out report.md # everything else, once a day ``` `sources` writes a report only when there is a new name. `daily` with `--skip x,hf` lists what `sources` kept in the last 24 hours. If you run only once a day, use `python -m radar daily` and skip nothing. Other flags: `--skip` takes any of `x,hf,breakout,sitemaps,newsites,gsc,review,judge,usecases`; `--new-sites` runs the weekly signal today; `--mail` sends the report (below); `--state DIR` moves the database and snapshots. ## What a report looks like From a real run on 2026-10-12 (shortened): ``` ### Candidate new terms (names first; terms you already cover are marked) | Term | Signals | Name score | Known | Search variants | Examples | | **gridcraft** | GitHub breakout storytold/gridcraft ★3178 (626/day) | 0.95 | none | storytold gridcraft | GridCraft: an open-source, cl… | | **artex** | GitHub breakout mhtsec/ARTEX ★3353 (825/day) | 0.85 | none | mhtsec artex, mht artex | AI 自主渗透测试系统 … | Other rising terms (judged common words): anatomy, math, iphone use ### ⑤ Review (terms reported 14 days ago: did they rise in DataForSEO Trends?) | Term | First reported | Verdict | Days ahead | | strata | 2026-09-25 | hit | 3 | ``` and from `sources`: ``` | **qwen image 2.1** | Hugging Face: new at #4, 2 versions | 1.00 | none | Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo (text-to-image, ♥569) | | **ltx 2.5** | Hugging Face: new at #6 | 0.90 | none | Lightricks/LTX-2.5 (image-to-video, ♥7347) | ``` `daily` also writes `report.json` beside the Markdown, with everything the report was built from. ## config.json | Key | What it is | |---|---| | `lang` | `"en"` or `"zh"`: the language of the report | | `x_accounts` | `labs` and `bloggers`: X handles to read. Labs say names first; pick the bloggers your field's new terms spread through | | `sitemaps` | Sites whose new pages you want to see. `index` is a sitemap, or a sitemap index when `shards` (a regex) picks which sub-sitemaps to read. `pause` is the seconds between requests to that site. `strip_locale` drops `/en/`, `/zh-CN/` prefixes so one entry in many languages counts once | | `topics` | Name and regex: each topic gets its own section listing the leads, repos and queries that match | | `known_terms` | Terms you already have a page for, or never want reported. A lead that contains one, or is contained in one, is marked and not kept for review | | `stop_words` | Everyday words of your field, added to the built-in list (which is tuned for AI tooling) | | `judge` | `model` (any chat model on AIsa) and `min_score` (0.5) | | `breakout` | `window_days`, `min_stars`, `velocity_min` (stars a day), `delta_min` (stars since yesterday) | | `new_sites` | `queries`: a name and a SQL LIKE pattern on the domain (`"%ai%"`), one paid query each; `weekday` (0 = Monday) | | `review` | `after_days` (14) and `per_day` (5 leads a day) | | `usecases` | The keyword table. `per_day` (names read a day, 0 = off), `model`, `benchmark` (the keyword sizes are compared with), `min_volume` (monthly searches a phrase needs), `min_daily` (searches a day for "prioritize"), `recheck_days` (3), `related` (use related queries when `GOANYAPI_API_KEY` is set), `related_geo` (`US`), `country_trends` (read the bigger rows' curves from that country), `country_min_volume` (1000) and `country_max` (8) | | `word_age` | `enabled`, `time_range` (`past_5_years`, the longest the Trends source offers), `new_days` (180: first searched within this many days = 🆕, read one step easier on page one) | | `markets` | `enabled`, `codes` (`["US", "DE", "FR", "JP"]`; built in: US, GB, CA, AU, IN, DE, FR, ES, IT, NL, BR, JP, KR), `difficulty` (per-market keyword difficulty), `top_region` (the Trends top country), `locations` (more markets: `{"MX": [2484, "es"]}`, a Google Ads location code and a language) | | `serp_shape` | `enabled`, `location_code` (2840), `language_code` (`en`), `device` (`desktop`), `platforms` (domains that count as high-authority platforms; `*.github.io` means its subdomains) | | `yours` | `enabled`, `domains` (your sites; empty = the Search Console property's domain), `days` (28: the Search Console window) | | `year_curve` | `enabled`: the twelve-month column, from the volume call (free) | | `dot_com` | `enabled`, `max_rows` (8: prioritized rows checked a run, names first) | | `ai_answers` | `enabled` (`false`: it costs about $0.004 an answer), `engines` (`["chatgpt"]`; add `"google"` for AI Mode), `max_rows` (6), `prompt` (`"What is the best tool to {job}?"`), `location_code` (2840), `language_code` (`en`) | | `gsc` | `site` (`sc-domain:example.com`) and `token_file`. Leave `{}` to turn the signal off; with it set, `yours` also reads your average position per keyword | Please read each site's robots.txt before you add its sitemap, and keep `pause` at or above its crawl-delay. The example config makes a few dozen requests a day in total, spaced by `pause`. ### Search Console (optional) ```bash pip install google-auth-oauthlib python scripts/gsc_auth.py gsc_client.json # opens a browser once, writes gsc_token.json ``` `gsc_client.json` is an OAuth client of type "Desktop app" from Google Cloud Console, in a project with the Search Console API enabled. Then set `"gsc": {"site": "sc-domain:your-site.com"}`. The token is read-only and stays on your machine; `.gitignore` already lists it. ### Mail (optional) `--mail` sends the report through [Resend](https://resend.com). Set `RESEND_API_KEY`, `EMAIL_FROM` (an address on a domain you verified there) and `RADAR_EMAIL_TO` (comma-separated). `pip install markdown` for the HTML version. ## Use it from an agent: skills and an MCP server ### Skills Three [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io/home) live in `skills/`: one that does the whole job, and the two halves for those who want them apart. | Skill | What it does | |---|---| | `new-term-radar` | The whole run: today's new names, then the keyword priority table for them. Also takes names you already have. Start here | | `ai-listening` | Collects what is new in the last 24 hours across the signals, deduplicated, as one report of names | | `seo-new-keywords-research` | Takes names, or raw text that mentions them, and returns the keyword priority table: the generic terms behind each name, screened, sized and given a decision | ```bash npx skills add zhuyansen/new-term-radar ``` In Claude Code the three skills also install as a plugin: ``` /plugin marketplace add zhuyansen/new-term-radar /plugin install new-term-radar@new-term-radar ``` Then ask your agent for "today's new AI keywords", "an AI listening report" or "keyword research on PhotoCraft and SynthID Detector". The skills run the pinned release from PyPI (`uvx new-term-radar==0.6.1`), never a clone, keep their state in `~/new-term-radar`, tell you the cost and wait for your yes before any paid run, show you what would go out on your behalf (a post, a page, a submission, an email) and wait for your yes before sending it, treat what they read as data rather than instructions, and say when a table is incomplete. ### MCP server For clients that speak MCP (Claude Code, Cursor, Claude Desktop). With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) there is nothing to install first: ```json { "mcpServers": { "new-term-radar": { "command": "uvx", "args": ["--with", "mcp", "new-term-radar", "mcp"], "env": { "AISA_API_KEY": "...", "RADAR_CONFIG": "/absolute/path/to/config.json", "RADAR_STATE": "/absolute/path/to/state" } } } } ``` Without uv: `pip install "new-term-radar[mcp]"`, then `"command": "new-term-radar-mcp"` and no `args`. The Claude Code plugin above brings this server with it: when the plugin is enabled, Claude Code asks for your AIsa key (and, optionally, a GoAnyAPI key) and keeps them in the system keychain; the server reads the example config and keeps its state in the plugin's data folder. | Tool | What it returns | Cost and time | |---|---|---| | `recent_leads` | What the radar kept, with review verdicts and the hit rate per signal | free, instant | | `keyword_table` | The keyword table for names you give it | about $0.05 a name plus $0.09 a call; 40 to 90 seconds a name | | `run_radar` | One `sources` or `daily` run and its report | paid; minutes. For a first try: the schedule belongs in cron or Actions | Point `RADAR_STATE` at the directory your scheduled runs write to and `recent_leads` shows their leads. The same two commands exist on the command line: `python -m radar keywords "name" …` and `python -m radar leads`. ### Codex, TRAE, WorkBuddy and DeepSeek Harness The same skills and server work in these agents too. Each starts the server with uvx, so [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) has to be installed. **Codex.** The skills: `npx skills add zhuyansen/new-term-radar -a codex` (add `-g` for every project). The server goes in `~/.codex/config.toml`, which the CLI, the IDE extension and the app share: ```toml [mcp_servers.new-term-radar] command = "uvx" args = ["--with", "mcp", "new-term-radar", "mcp"] startup_timeout_sec = 120 tool_timeout_sec = 900 [mcp_servers.new-term-radar.env] AISA_API_KEY = "..." RADAR_STATE = "/absolute/path/to/state" ``` Codex gives a server 10 seconds to start and a tool 60 seconds to answer. The first start downloads the package, `keyword_table` takes 40 to 90 seconds a name and a `daily` run 5 to 15 minutes, so raise both as above. `codex mcp add new-term-radar --env AISA_API_KEY=... --env RADAR_STATE=/absolute/path/to/state -- uvx --with mcp new-term-radar mcp` writes the same entry without the two timeouts. **TRAE.** The skills: `npx skills add zhuyansen/new-term-radar -a trae` (TRAE CN: `-a trae-cn`). The server: Settings → MCP → Add → Add manually, and paste the JSON above. In TRAE CN you can instead paste this link into the browser's address bar; TRAE opens the server's configuration, where you fill in your AIsa key and an absolute path for `RADAR_STATE`, and confirm: ```text trae-cn://trae.ai-ide/mcp-import?type=stdio&name=new-term-radar&config=eyJjb21tYW5kIjoidXZ4IiwiYXJncyI6WyItLXdpdGgiLCJtY3AiLCJuZXctdGVybS1yYWRhciIsIm1jcCJdLCJlbnYiOnsiQUlTQV9BUElfS0VZIjoiIiwiR09BTllBUElfQVBJX0tFWSI6IiIsIlJBREFSX1NUQVRFIjoiL2Fic29sdXRlL3BhdGgvdG8vc3RhdGUifX0%3D ``` **WorkBuddy.** Put the JSON above in `~/.workbuddy/mcp.json`, or paste it under Plugins → MCP servers → Configure MCP. **DeepSeek Harness.** The skills: `npx skills add zhuyansen/new-term-radar -a codex` installs them in `.agents/skills` (with `-g`, in `~/.agents/skills`), where DeepSeek Harness looks too. The server goes in `~/.dsh/cordis.patch.yml` for every profile, or `~/.dsh/profiles//cordis.patch.yml` for one: ```yaml - insert: - id: new-term-radar name: '@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client' config: serverName: new-term-radar transport: stdio command: uvx args: ['--with', 'mcp', 'new-term-radar', 'mcp'] env: AISA_API_KEY: !!js process.env.AISA_API_KEY ?? '' GOANYAPI_API_KEY: !!js process.env.GOANYAPI_API_KEY ?? '' RADAR_STATE: /absolute/path/to/state toolCallTimeoutMs: 900000 ``` DeepSeek Harness does not pass the variables that look like keys on to a server, so the keys are named under `env`, read here from your environment. Keep the `?? ''`: without it a variable that is not set fails the entry's check and the server does not start; an empty key counts as no key. A tool gets 60 seconds unless `toolCallTimeoutMs` gives more; a `daily` run needs the 15 minutes above. `dsh web --dump-config` prints the composed entry without starting anything. Tried with DeepSeek Harness 0.2.1-rc.2. ## Run it on GitHub Actions `.github/workflows/radar.yml` runs `sources` every 8 hours and `daily` once a day, keeps the state in the Actions cache, and writes each report to the run summary. It is off until you opt in: 1. Fork the repository (a private fork is fine). 2. Remove `config.json` from `.gitignore` and commit your config. It holds no secrets. 3. Add the secret `AISA_API_KEY`; optionally `GOANYAPI_API_KEY`, `RESEND_API_KEY`, `EMAIL_FROM`, `RADAR_EMAIL_TO`, `GSC_TOKEN_JSON`. 4. Set the repository variable `RADAR_ENABLED` to `true`. ## How the pieces decide - **Names in posts** (`radar/terms.py`): capitalised words, words with a digit (`Qwen3.8`) or inner capitals (`HyperFrames`); a number after a name joins it (`Opus 5.5`). A name two accounts used counts; a name one account used needs 100 likes and must be unmistakably a name, since a capitalised word is often just the start of a sentence. - **Surges in sitemaps**: counted per distinct URL against the site's own baseline, so one page with a long slug cannot fake a wave. - **The judge** (`radar/judge.py`): one chat call per 25 terms, each with up to three places it appeared. If the call fails the report still goes out, unsorted. - **The review** (`radar/review.py`): a variant counts as "rose" when its peak after the day we reported it clears its own earlier baseline by 2x and by 10 points. A word with an older meaning ("strata": rock layers, property law) has a high baseline and does not count; "niko1221 strata" going from 0 to something does. Trends' unsettled last two days are left out. ## What we measured, and what we have not - The name judge (`gpt-4.1-mini`) was run on 170 terms an earlier judge had passed as names in our own daily use. It agreed on 149. Of the 21 it rejected, most were noise the earlier judge let through (sitemap path fragments such as `io.github.wxt invoice`, `asd`); about three were real names it missed (`synthid detector`, `veo`, `v4.1 flash`), in a test that gave it less context than a real run does. It passed none of 40 common words (`dashboard`, `pricing`, `today`). - Hit rates per signal: not yet. The review needs 14 days per lead and ours has only begun. The one seeded check, Strata, came back a hit, three days ahead of its Trends rise. Your own report shows your numbers as they accumulate; treat any signal as unproven until then. - The X signal is only as good as the account list. It will not see a name none of your accounts says. ## Known issues - The built-in stop words and the Hugging Face name cleaning are tuned for AI models and agent tooling. For another field, add `stop_words`. - Search volumes are not in the report. The radar tells you a name is new; check volume and the top results before you build a page for it. ## Development ```bash pip install pytest markdown python -m pytest -q tests ``` The tests cover the logic (name extraction, scoring, the store, the reports) and call no network. ## Thanks - Thanks to [哥飞 @gefei55](https://x.com/gefei55) for the groundwork: the radar is built on what he lays out in his WeChat articles and on his way of looking for signals on social media first, together with how I find sources from running my own social media accounts. - [子木 @CoderJeffLee](https://x.com/CoderJeffLee) for the idea behind the keyword table: a new name and the generic terms downstream of it belong in one table, each with a decision. - [饭特稀 | Fentix @fantexi997](https://x.com/fantexi997) for [GoAnyAPI](https://goanyapi.com), the optional source of related queries and one-country Trends series. The diagram is drawn by `docs/make_diagram.py` (needs `rsvg-convert` and `ffmpeg`). ## Star history [![Star history](https://api.star-history.com/svg?repos=zhuyansen/new-term-radar&type=Date)](https://star-history.com/#zhuyansen/new-term-radar&Date) ## License MIT. A daily report of the names that are starting to surge in AI: new models, products, tools and repos, caught where they are said first, before they show up in keyword tools.

Built for people who make pages, posts or products around new terms: SEO for AI tool sites, newsletters, directories, anyone who wants to know about "Strata" or "Seedance" the day it appears and not two weeks later.

Why

A new name leaves a trail, in this order:

1. A lab or a well-followed account says it on X; a model enters Hugging Face's trending list.

2. One GitHub repo takes off on its own.

3. Directories and competitors add pages for it; someone registers a domain for it and the site starts to rank.

4. Your own site gets its first search impressions for it.

5. Google Trends shows the curve, days or weeks later.

Keyword tools read step 5. This radar reads steps 1 to 4 every day and uses step 5 only to check itself.

One example it was built around: Niko1221/Strata was created on 2026-09-24 and had 7,700 stars nine days later. People were searching "niko strata" from 9/26, while no second repo carried the name and no keyword tool listed it. A single repo gaining 800 stars a day is the whole signal, and it is public.

What it reads

How it is made (radar/usecases.py):

1. Evidence: the most-liked posts that mention the name (X advanced search) and, for a repository, its README.

2. Phrases: a model reads the evidence and writes the keyword an ordinary person would type for each job it sees people doing, with a quote that backs it. A phrase built on another product's name ("photoshop alternative") is kept and marked ⚠: demand often hangs on the incumbent, and whether to use someone's brand is your call.

With a GoAnyAPI key (optional, below) the radar also takes Google Trends' related queries for the name: what people really searched together with it. For SynthID Detector that gave "ai photo detector", "google ai detector" and "ai detector"; these rows carry 🔎. Queries that hold the name are listed as its long-tails ("photocraft download", "nano banana 2.1 vs pro"). Queries that are themselves the names of other rising things ("gpt image 2.5" beside "nano banana 2.1") are kept as leads of their own.

3. Screen: a second call scores how well the name answers each phrase, marks brands, and spots the names of other things; the loosely related ones are dropped. For Claude Haiku 5.5 it dropped all six proposed ("ai coding assistant", "github copilot alternative"); for SynthID Detector it kept all five.

4. Volume: Google Ads monthly searches for the rest, one batch call. Phrases under min_volume are dropped; most are.

5. Trends, twice per row: the term alone gives the shape (new or not, the day it started rising, the peak, the last week against the week before, what it is doing now); the term beside a benchmark keyword (gpts by default) gives the size.

6. Page one, for the rows that would be acted on (eight at most): Google's first page (about $0.002 a keyword), the rating of each site on it (GoAnyAPI, $0.002 a site, kept 30 days) and the keyword difficulty ($0.012 a call). With a GoAnyAPI key also who already builds for the term and who pays for it: the pages Google holds with it in the title from the last month (pages built) and the domains running Google ads on it (advertisers, from Ads transparency), $0.008 a row. open = three or more of the ten results sit on sites rated under 30, or difficulty under 20; crowded = none does and difficulty is 40 or more; mixed in between. Under the table it names the weakest site on page one, where a new page can get in, and what kinds of pages hold it (tools, lists, articles, videos, forums). Ads on the page mean someone pays for that click. Recorded only, in report.json as page_age and not used in any decision yet: how old the sites on page one are (each domain's registration, from RDAP, free) and which results entered the top 10 since the reading before, to check later whether a page one with young sites on it is one a new site gets onto.

7. Word age, for the prioritize and watch rows: the term's Trends interest over five years (one point a week); the first week with any interest is First searched, and 🆕 marks a term first searched in the last 180 days. A new term's page one is read one step easier (crowded → mixed, mixed → open): difficulty scores and site ratings are made from pages written for something else and lag a word nobody searched half a year ago. The week still running and Trends' unsettled last two days are left out, so a "0, 100" tail cannot make an old word look new. One Trends task a row, $0.0012. A term made of words people searched before ("nano banana" reads a little interest in 2021) is dated by those older searches.

8. Markets, for the same rows: Google Ads monthly searches in each market of markets.codes (US, DE, FR, JP by default; all languages) and, with difficulty on, the keyword difficulty there, in one compact cell: best DE · US 5k/50 · DE 900/5 · FR 300 · JP 0 · top Germany. best = the most searches per point of difficulty when every market with searches has a difficulty, else the most searches. top = the country where Trends interest is highest, among the major markets (Trends measures a share of local searches, and on its own puts Sint Maarten first). About $0.41 a run with the defaults (a $0.09 volume call per market, about $0.012 a difficulty call), plus $0.0024 a row for the top region.

9. Page-one shape, for the prioritized rows: the live top ten (US / en / desktop by default; the page-one check's own results are reused, so it usually costs nothing extra, otherwise about $0.002 a term) read as homepages against inner pages, results on high-authority platforms (serp_shape.platforms: github.com, medium.com, sites.google.com, *.github.io, reddit.com, youtube.com, wikipedia.org) and titles that hold the keyword. platform-held = half or more on platforms; beatable = mostly inner pages and no exact-match homepage (a homepage titled with the term, or whose domain spells it); contested otherwise. Under the table it lists the URL and title of #1 and #2.

Each of the three has "enabled": false in its config block to turn it off. On 2026-10-18, for "photocraft" (prioritize) and "ai image detector" (watch), they read: first searched 2026-10-04 🆕 and 2023-02-19; best market US for both (74k searches and KD 37 for "ai image detector"); page one of "photocraft" beatable · 1 home / 6 inner · 2 platform · exact title ×6, held at #1 by the GitHub repository. The run cost $0.42.

Four more readings came in 0.6.0 too. None of them buys anything: they read what the volume call and the page-one check already brought back, your own Search Console, and the .com registry.

10. 12 months (year_curve), every row with Google Ads data: the volume call already carries each phrase's last twelve months. The column draws them as bars on the term's own scale from zero and adds a word: new since (barely searched a year ago), peaked (a burst past its top: twice its median month or more, at half of it or less now), falling, rising (the last three months against the three before, ±30%) or steady; under 50 searches in its best month it says few searches, since Google Ads rounds small volumes. The newest month is one to two months behind. On 2026-10-20 "claude skills" read peaked 2026-03, now -80% (90,500 a month at the top, 18,100 in 2026-09), "best claude skills" new since 2026-01 · falling, -47% in 6 mo, and "skill md" steady.

11. Your rank (yours), for the prioritize and watch rows: your sites (yours.domains, else the domain of the Search Console property in gsc.site) looked for in the page-one check's ten results and, with gsc set, in Search Console (average position, impressions and clicks for the exact query over 28 days, one call for all rows). The decision cell then says what to do: → update yours (on page one by either), → improve yours (a Search Console average of 11 to 30), → new page (not found, or further down), and your pages are listed under the table. A rising term you already rank for is an update, not a new page. On 2026-10-20 one of our sites showed for one term at an average of 23.5 (improve that page) and for another at 89 with one impression, on its homepage (a new page).

12. What else holds page one, from the page-one check: its cell now names an AI overview, an answer box, a forums block, videos or news, and under the table come the forum threads on page one, best-of searches first: an answer there reaches the people searching. When Google shows an AI summary, people click a result about half as often (Pew Research Center, 2025: on 8% of visits against 15%). All five "claude skills" terms read on 2026-10-20 had an AI overview.

13. Exact-match .com (dot_com), for the prioritized rows, names first: the joined and hyphenated forms asked of the registry's RDAP (Verisign), free. Not registered is not always the usual price: registrars hold some names back or sell them as premium. Of the ten forms of five "claude skills" terms, one was free on 2026-10-20.

Each has "enabled" in its own config block; the page-one marks come with the page-one check. On 2026-10-20 five terms cost $0.11 in all, which was the volume call and the page-one check.

Searches a day are estimates. A generic term's come from its own Google Ads volume, moved to today along its own Trends curve. The benchmark is then sized from those terms, and a name, which has no volume data yet, is sized against the benchmark.

Decision: prioritize = rose in the last 30 days, still up, at least min_daily searches a day. watch = rose but smaller, too early to read, or flat with steady demand of that size. skip = fading, or flat and small. A prioritize whose page one is crowded becomes watch ↓: still rising, but page one belongs to strong sites. In a name's first week page one is still forming (news, the maker's own pages); the second reading three days later is the one to trust.

Marks: 🎬 video, 🎙 voice, 🖼 image says what the thing makes, the usual order of what visitors pay for (video > voice > image > text); leads of equal standing are sorted by it. ⚡ = a post with 1,000 or more likes walks through a manual workflow or rides a trend: a one-click tool nobody has built yet. Both come from keyword rules over the lead's own words and posts; on six known names (Nano Banana, Veo 3.1, Seedance 2.5, Claude Opus 5.5, ElevenLabs v4, Qwen Image 2.1) the format came out right for all six and ⚡ fired once, on a widely shared Opus 5.5 + Blender + Unreal walkthrough. Read the posts before acting on a mark.

Each name is read twice, the day it appears and three days later, because on announcement day the posts are announcements and no use shows yet. The generic terms are kept as leads and reviewed after 14 days like the names.

What to expect from it, from the first eight names we ran it on:

  • The names rose; most generic terms did not, within five days. PhotoCraft, Claude Haiku 5.5 and SynthID Detector all climbed clearly. Of the generic terms behind them, one moved: "photoshop alternative" ran about 80% above its level in the US for five days after PhotoCraft appeared. The worldwide daily series the table reads showed almost nothing of it (2, 1, 1, 2, 4, 2); a US daily series from another source showed it plainly. So a flat reading from the worldwide series does not prove a term did not move. With a GoAnyAPI key the bigger rows are read from the one-country series instead, where a rise is 1.5 times the earlier level held for three days; the same run then shows "photoshop alternative" as still rising (US).
  • The table's dependable use today is to tell you which existing demand a new thing serves and how big it is ("ai image detector", about 2,500 searches a day). Whether generic terms follow the names is what the 14-day review will show, and we have no result yet.
  • For pure model releases (Claude Haiku 5.5, Nano Banana 2.1) the evidence was announcements and benchmarks, and the phrases proposed were weak ("ai coding assistant"). It works better for products and repositories that do one job.
  • The worldwide Trends series' last two days are not settled. For unrelated terms they came back as 0 and then 100, which reads as a spike. Our first pass was fooled by exactly this; every reader in the code now drops those two days, and a rise must last two days to count.
  • Google Ads volumes run about two months behind. Trends reads nothing reliable for terms under a few hundred searches a month.

⑥ Revenue: what people already pay for

A product that makes money proves the demand behind it. With TRUSTMRR_API_KEY set (from TrustMRR's developer dashboard), the radar reads once a week (revenue.weekday, Monday by default) the 30 fastest-growing products with at least min_revenue_usd ($500) in the last 30 days and the 30 newest listings, and keeps what it saw. The newest listings mostly earn next to nothing yet; they are read to record where they start, so a product at $0 last time that earns past the floor now is called out first. Hidden listings ("Anonymous startup") are left out, and a company's legal name gives way to its site's name ("Talent Tech Global Limited" is read as gptproto). Each product's own description goes to the keyword table as evidence, so the table reads the job people pay for, not only the brand. Growth above 1,000% reads "up from near $0": on the first run most of the fastest growers had started from almost nothing.

TrustMRR's API terms forbid republishing its data and building public SEO pages from it. Use the leads for your own research; do not publish the list.

⑦ Asks: demand said out loud

Once a week the radar searches Reddit for a dozen ways people ask for a tool ("is there an AI tool", "I wish there was a tool", "how do I automate", in asks.patterns), keeps the posts of the last week with a score of 2 or more, and has a small model sort them: a request, a complaint, a shared solution, or other. For requests and complaints an AI tool could answer, it writes the job the way a person would search it ("add b roll automatically", "convert slides to notes"). Jobs with at least 50 searches a month are listed with their posts and get the page-one check; each becomes a lead. Most asks are too specific to have searches yet: the first real week, 84 posts held 43 asks and only two had 50 searches a month ("best ai tool for research", from a 1,034-point r/PhD thread, and "best ai tool for coding"). So the best-scored of the others are listed too, as ideas rather than keywords. A month of posts read in a trial held a request for "an AI tool to convert PowerPoint lecture slides into notes", the same job a tool-site course uses as its worked example.

With ai_answers on (off by default; about $0.004 an answer), the jobs with searches are also put to ChatGPT, as the answer its own interface gives with search (DataForSEO's LLM scraper), and with "engines": ["chatgpt", "google"] to Google's AI Mode, as "What is the best tool to {job}?". A column says which tools the answers name; under the table come the sites they cite, and ✅ when one is yours. An answer that names no tool is a gap a new tool can fill in AI search; the cited sites are the pages AI search reads for the job: get listed there, or write the comparison against them. On 2026-10-20, for "convert powerpoint slides to notes", ChatGPT named Google NotebookLM, ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot, and AI Mode listed Knowt, NoteGPT and Microsoft Copilot among others.

Posts are for your own research: quote them, do not republish them.

⑧ Sellers: who just started taking money

A product's first payment link says more than its launch post: someone built a thing and asked for money for it. whoismaking.money used to rank sites by the traffic they sent to Stripe's checkout (clickstream data; its last real page in the Internet Archive is from September 2025, and by March 2026 the domain served a parked page with a hidden redirect). The same kind of data is on sale through AIsa's Similarweb at about $6 for 20 rows: too dear to cover the long tail. Payment links are a cheap stand-in. They are ordinary links on the seller's own page, so the public link graph shows them with the day each first appeared. Stripe has 143,000 linking sites and Polar 1,900 (every link a payment link); for Lemon Squeezy, Gumroad and Creem only store checkouts, /l/ products and /payment/ pages count, since their other links point at their own marketing sites and, for Gumroad, at profile pages spam networks use.

Once a week the radar reads, for each platform, the newest 100 payment links and the newest 100 sites to link to it for the first time (about $0.06 a platform), keeps the links of those new sites, and lists the sellers with their visits (GoAnyAPI) and their own home-page title and description, which also go to the keyword table as evidence. The first real run put janitorai.com, framer.com, pub.dev, Flathub and an n8n forum thread on top: user pages on big platforms that link to someone's payment link. So the linking page must be the site's own home, pricing or product page, not a post, thread or listing; the site must rank 350 or lower on DataForSEO's 0 to 1,000 scale; and above 300,000 visits a month it counts as a platform. A small model then sorts the new sellers by kind from their own words (keyword rules when it cannot), and AI and software come first, then templates, courses and the rest; within a kind the busiest first. On the first sorted run all twelve listed were software (a live-captions app for the Mac, a chat-with-PDF tool, an AI writing app for macOS, an MCP catalog, a Japanese audit SaaS among them), where traffic alone had put a Blender add-on site, a recipe blog and a design gallery first. A payment link means the site sells, not that it sells well, and checkouts made by code at payment time are not seen.

A new link is not a new seller. A first version took the newest links for new sellers; on 2026-10-14 we checked them against the day each site first linked to the platform. A site that has sold for years puts the same link on every new page it makes (one carries its Stripe link on each of its well-permit pages), and two thirds of the 2,000 newest Stripe links came from such sites: of the 60 Stripe sellers that day's list showed, 17 had just started. So a seller is new by the day its site first linked to the platform (DataForSEO's referring domains), and the report says how many links came from sites that sold already.

  • low-star Chrome Web Store reviews (1 to 3 stars) of the extensions Google shows for the keyword, or of the ones you name with --extension ID (GoAnyAPI: 2 credits to find them, 3 a page of reviews);
  • Reddit posts that complain about the job or its tools ("{keyword} alternative", "{keyword} frustrating", ...; AIsa);
  • comments under the top tutorial videos for the keyword (AIsa).

A model groups them into gaps (missing, too hard, quality, price, wants a tool), each with a count, an example and the phrase someone with that problem would search. About $0.05 a keyword. Counts are of what was read, not of the market.

What it cannot read: App Store, Google Play and Trustpilot reviews (DataForSEO serves them as tasks to post and fetch later, and AIsa runs synchronous calls only); There's An AI For That's request board (a Cloudflare challenge in front of every page; getting past it would be getting past their bot protection, so the radar does not); Facebook groups (Meta closed the Groups API in April 2024, and its research library is open to approved academic and nonprofit researchers only).

One key, and an optional second

Everything the radar needs goes through AIsa: X posts, DataForSEO Trends (DataForSEO's estimate of Google search interest, not Google Trends itself) and domain data, and the models that judge names and propose phrases. One key, pay per call, no subscriptions to X's API or DataForSEO.

> That link is a referral link: signing up through it supports this project. The radar works the same with a key from anywhere on aisa.one.

Optional: GOANYAPI_API_KEY (goanyapi.com) improves the keyword table in two ways, for about $0.07 a day: it adds Google Trends' related queries for each name, and it reads the curve of the names and the bigger generic terms (1,000 searches a month or more, eight rows at most) from 30 days of daily data for one country, settled to yesterday. Those rows show the country after "Now", as in still rising (US). Without the key the table is built from the model's phrases and the worldwide series alone. The service is young (first released in August 2026); in our tests calls took 20 to 55 seconds and about one in ten failed, so the radar tries twice, reports a failure in the table and carries on. That link is a referral link too.

Without an AIsa key the free signals still run (Hugging Face, GitHub, sitemaps, Search Console); the report then lists every term unsorted, because nothing judges which are names.

Quick start

uv's uvx runs the radar straight from PyPI, with nothing to clone or install:


export AISA_API_KEY=...                       # from https://go.aisa.one/yansen-zhu; or `aisa login` with the AIsa CLI

uvx new-term-radar daily --out report.md      # today's new names and the keyword table behind them

uvx new-term-radar keywords "photocraft"      # the keyword table for names you already have

With no config.json in the folder, daily watches the example X accounts and sitemaps that ship with the radar and keeps its snapshots in ./state; copy [config.example.json](config.example.json) to config.json there and edit it to watch your own. uvx new-term-radar@latest … picks up a new release; pip install new-term-radar (or uv tool install new-term-radar) keeps a new-term-radar command installed. Python 3.10 or newer; the radar uses only the standard library.

From a clone it is the same program, with the same key:


git clone https://github.com/zhuyansen/new-term-radar

cd new-term-radar

cp config.example.json config.json      # then edit: your X accounts, sitemaps, topics

python -m radar daily --out report.md

The first run builds its snapshots: yesterday's X vocabulary, star counts and sitemap URLs do not exist yet, so only GitHub breakouts (which need no yesterday) are reported. From the second run on, every signal reports what changed.

Two commands (without a clone, uvx new-term-radar in place of python -m radar):


python -m radar sources --out sources.md           # ① only: X and Hugging Face. Run every few hours.

python -m radar daily --skip x,hf --out report.md  # everything else, once a day

sources writes a report only when there is a new name. daily with --skip x,hf lists what sources kept in the last 24 hours. If you run only once a day, use python -m radar daily and skip nothing.

Other flags: --skip takes any of x,hf,breakout,sitemaps,newsites,gsc,review,judge,usecases; --new-sites runs the weekly signal today; --mail sends the report (below); --state DIR moves the database and snapshots.

config.json

| Key | What it is |

|---|---|

| lang | "en" or "zh": the language of the report |

| x_accounts | labs and bloggers: X handles to read. Labs say names first; pick the bloggers your field's new terms spread through |

| sitemaps | Sites whose new pages you want to see. index is a sitemap, or a sitemap index when shards (a regex) picks which sub-sitemaps to read. pause is the seconds between requests to that site. strip_locale drops /en/, /zh-CN/ prefixes so one entry in many languages counts once |

| topics | Name and regex: each topic gets its own section listing the leads, repos and queries that match |

| known_terms | Terms you already have a page for, or never want reported. A lead that contains one, or is contained in one, is marked and not kept for review |

| stop_words | Everyday words of your field, added to the built-in list (which is tuned for AI tooling) |

| judge | model (any chat model on AIsa) and min_score (0.5) |

| breakout | window_days, min_stars, velocity_min (stars a day), delta_min (stars since yesterday) |

| new_sites | queries: a name and a SQL LIKE pattern on the domain ("%ai%"), one paid query each; weekday (0 = Monday) |

| review | after_days (14) and per_day (5 leads a day) |

| usecases | The keyword table. per_day (names read a day, 0 = off), model, benchmark (the keyword sizes are compared with), min_volume (monthly searches a phrase needs), min_daily (searches a day for "prioritize"), recheck_days (3), related (use related queries when GOANYAPI_API_KEY is set), related_geo (US), country_trends (read the bigger rows' curves from that country), country_min_volume (1000) and country_max (8) |

| word_age | enabled, time_range (past_5_years, the longest the Trends source offers), new_days (180: first searched within this many days = 🆕, read one step easier on page one) |

| markets | enabled, codes (["US", "DE", "FR", "JP"]; built in: US, GB, CA, AU, IN, DE, FR, ES, IT, NL, BR, JP, KR), difficulty (per-market keyword difficulty), top_region (the Trends top country), locations (more markets: {"MX": [2484, "es"]}, a Google Ads location code and a language) |

| serp_shape | enabled, location_code (2840), language_code (en), device (desktop), platforms (domains that count as high-authority platforms; *.github.io means its subdomains) |

| yours | enabled, domains (your sites; empty = the Search Console property's domain), days (28: the Search Console window) |

| year_curve | enabled: the twelve-month column, from the volume call (free) |

| dot_com | enabled, max_rows (8: prioritized rows checked a run, names first) |

| ai_answers | enabled (false: it costs about $0.004 an answer), engines (["chatgpt"]; add "google" for AI Mode), max_rows (6), prompt ("What is the best tool to {job}?"), location_code (2840), language_code (en) |

How the pieces decide

  • Names in posts (radar/terms.py): capitalised words, words with a digit (Qwen3.8) or inner capitals (HyperFrames); a number after a name joins it (Opus 5.5). A name two accounts used counts; a name one account used needs 100 likes and must be unmistakably a name, since a capitalised word is often just the start of a sentence.
  • Surges in sitemaps: counted per distinct URL against the site's own baseline, so one page with a long slug cannot fake a wave.
  • The judge (radar/judge.py): one chat call per 25 terms, each with up to three places it appeared. If the call fails the report still goes out, unsorted.
  • The review (radar/review.py): a variant counts as "rose" when its peak after the day we reported it clears its own earlier baseline by 2x and by 10 points. A word with an older meaning ("strata": rock layers, property law) has a high baseline and does not count; "niko1221 strata" going from 0 to something does. Trends' unsettled last two days are left out.

What we measured, and what we have not

  • The name judge (gpt-4.1-mini) was run on 170 terms an earlier judge had passed as names in our own daily use. It agreed on 149. Of the 21 it rejected, most were noise the earlier judge let through (sitemap path fragments such as io.github.wxt invoice, asd); about three were real names it missed (synthid detector, veo, v4.1 flash), in a test that gave it less context than a real run does. It passed none of 40 common words (dashboard, pricing, today).
  • Hit rates per signal: not yet. The review needs 14 days per lead and ours has only begun. The one seeded check, Strata, came back a hit, three days ahead of its Trends rise. Your own report shows your numbers as they accumulate; treat any signal as unproven until then.
  • The X signal is only as good as the account list. It will not see a name none of your accounts says.

Known issues

  • The built-in stop words and the Hugging Face name cleaning are tuned for AI models and agent tooling. For another field, add stop_words.
  • Search volumes are not in the report. The radar tells you a name is new; check volume and the top results before you build a page for it.
